R0269.title: Teleoperation Channel Hijacking Attack
R0269.definition: An attack where the attacker hijacks, replays, or injects control commands on a robot teleoperation (teleop) channel to remotely manipulate the robot into unintended actions, or injects latency and jitter to destabilize fine operations.
R0269.description:
Teleoperation channel hijacking targets the remote-control links of humanoid, surgical, and hazardous-operation robots. The University of Washington team first performed experimental attacks on the Raven II open-source remote surgical robot in 2015, able to trigger emergency stops, perform man-in-the-middle attacks, and tamper with control commands. Teleoperation is latency-sensitive; research shows 0–500 ms delays significantly affect teleoperation performance and operator neuro-cognitive response, so an attacker injecting communication latency can destabilize precise operations. Action-replay attacks intercept legitimate control commands and replay them so the robot executes historical actions. A survey on quadruped-robot teleoperation security identifies its unique attack surface: dynamic-stability constraints, gait-dependent vulnerability windows, large kinetic energy, and high operator cognitive load.

This risk relates to R0142 (man-in-the-middle attack) and R0163 (smart-device hijacking), but is specialized for the low-latency and anti-replay requirements of real-time control channels; consequences can cause casualties (surgical robots) or major physical damage.
R0269.influence: Can remotely manipulate surgical, humanoid, or hazardous-operation robots to perform harmful actions, or destabilize precise operations; consequences can cause casualties or major property damage, making it a lethal threat to embodied intelligence in medical and high-risk scenarios.

references.title: To Make a Robot Secure: An Experimental Analysis of Cyber Security Threats Against Teleoperated Surgical Robots
